```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
has_sf <- requireNamespace("sf", quietly = TRUE)
has_cc <- requireNamespace("CoordinateCleaner", quietly = TRUE)
```

Seven tests compare records with reference data: four with points (capitals, centroids, institutions, the GBIF headquarters) and three with polygons (land, urban areas, countries). The package ships its own pinned layers for all of them, and `reference = "CoordinateCleaner"` swaps in CoordinateCleaner's. The `gazetteers` argument of `flag_occurrences()` replaces the layer of single tests with a user's own, as the `ref` arguments of CoordinateCleaner's `cc_*()` functions do. This article filters and extends the shipped point tables, builds polygon layers with sf, and shows how a custom layer is recorded with the flags.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(OccurrenceCleaner)
```

## The shipped points

`reference_points()` returns the points of a proximity test with their attributes:

```{r points}
caps <- reference_points("capital")
head(caps)
table(caps$class)
inst <- reference_points("institution")
head(sort(table(inst$type), decreasing = TRUE))
```

The institution table is the GBIF registry of scientific collections (GRSciColl): `type` says what kind of institution each is, and `master_source` where GBIF took the entry from (Index Herbariorum, GRSciColl itself, or the GBIF registry).

## A filtered point gazetteer

A point layer is any data frame with longitude and latitude columns (`lon`/`lat`, `longitude`/`latitude` or `decimalLongitude`/`decimalLatitude`, in any case). A plant study, for example, may want to flag records at herbaria only, since a specimen georeferenced to a zoological museum is unlikely in a plant table, and use a wider buffer for them:

```{r herbaria}
herbaria <- inst[inst$type %in% "Herbarium", ]
nrow(herbaria)
near <- rbind(herbaria[1:3, ], inst[inst$type %in% "Museum", ][1:3, ])
x <- data.frame(species = "Quercus robur", decimalLongitude = near$lon + 0.005,
                decimalLatitude = near$lat)
f_all <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = "institution", buffers = list(institution = 1000))
f_herb <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = "institution", buffers = list(institution = 1000),
                           gazetteers = list(institution = herbaria))
data.frame(near = near$name, type = near$type, all = f_all$flag_institution,
           herbaria_only = f_herb$flag_institution)
```

Each record lies about 0.005 degrees (a few hundred metres) east of an institution: three herbaria, then three museums. The full table flags all six at a 1 km buffer; the herbarium table flags only `r sum(f_herb$flag_institution)`, the records next to the herbaria.

## An extended point gazetteer

The two capital tables differ: the Natural Earth table lists alternative and official capitals, CoordinateCleaner's has one point per country, rounded to 0.01 degrees. Their union flags records near either:

```{r union, eval = has_cc}
both <- rbind(caps[, c("lon", "lat")], reference_points("capital", reference = "CoordinateCleaner"))
nrow(both)
y <- data.frame(city = c("Cape Town", "Naypyidaw", "Vienna"), decimalLongitude = c(18.42, 96.13, 16.37),
                decimalLatitude = c(-33.92, 19.75, 48.21))
data.frame(city = y$city,
           CoordinateCleaner = flag_occurrences(y, tests = "capital", reference = "CoordinateCleaner")$flag_capital,
           union = flag_occurrences(y, tests = "capital", gazetteers = list(capital = both))$flag_capital)
```

Other point sets fit the same way: regional capitals for a study in which collections were georeferenced to provincial seats, the field stations of a survey, or the coordinates a particular data provider uses as a default.

## Polygon layers

Polygon layers are `sf` or `sfc` objects of POLYGON or MULTIPOLYGON geometries in longitude and latitude (EPSG:4326). For `sea`, the polygons are the land: a record outside every polygon is flagged. That makes `sea` with a custom layer a test for "outside the study area":

```{r study-area, eval = has_sf}
area <- sf::st_sfc(sf::st_polygon(list(rbind(c(9.5, 46.4), c(17.2, 46.4), c(17.2, 49.0),
                                             c(9.5, 49.0), c(9.5, 46.4)))), crs = 4326)
z <- data.frame(decimalLongitude = c(16.37, 11.40, 8.54, 19.04), decimalLatitude = c(48.21, 47.26, 47.37, 47.50))
flag_occurrences(z, tests = "sea", gazetteers = list(sea = area))$flag_sea
```

The first two points (Vienna, Innsbruck) lie inside the box, the last two (Zurich, Budapest) outside it. The same applies to `urban`, whose polygons are the areas to flag, for example a city's built-up area at a finer scale than Natural Earth's.

For `country_mismatch` the polygons carry codes. Any of the columns `iso_a2`, `iso_a3`, `adm0_a3` or `code` (in any case) is read, and the record's code is matched against all of them. Two territories with their own codes:

```{r countries, eval = has_sf}
terr <- sf::st_sf(
  code = c("XA", "XB"),
  geometry = sf::st_sfc(sf::st_polygon(list(rbind(c(0, 0), c(10, 0), c(10, 10), c(0, 10), c(0, 0)))),
                        sf::st_polygon(list(rbind(c(10, 0), c(20, 0), c(20, 10), c(10, 10), c(10, 0)))),
                        crs = 4326))
w <- data.frame(decimalLongitude = c(5, 15, 15, 25), decimalLatitude = 5, countryCode = c("XA", "XB", "XA", "XA"))
flag_occurrences(w, tests = "country_mismatch", gazetteers = list(country_mismatch = terr))$flag_country_mismatch
```

The third record is in territory XB with code XA, the fourth outside both territories, so both are flagged.

## Recording the layer

A custom layer is indexed once per call, and its size and an MD5 checksum of its coordinates are written into the reference label of the output:

```{r label}
f <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = "institution", gazetteers = list(institution = herbaria))
attr(f, "occ_reference")
```

The checksum identifies the exact table, so two analyses that report the same label used the same points. For streamed input the label is stored in the output directory, and a rerun into that directory with a different custom layer stops with an error instead of mixing flags from two gazetteers.

## Comparison with CoordinateCleaner

```{r cc-map, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  CoordinateCleaner = c("cc_cap(ref = ...)", "cc_cen(ref = ...)", "cc_inst(ref = ...)",
                        "cc_sea(ref = ...)", "cc_urb(ref = ...)", "cc_coun(ref = ..., ref_col = ...)"),
  OccurrenceCleaner = c("gazetteers = list(capital = points)", "gazetteers = list(centroid = points)",
                        "gazetteers = list(institution = points)", "gazetteers = list(sea = polygons)",
                        "gazetteers = list(urban = polygons)", "gazetteers = list(country_mismatch = polygons)"),
  check.names = FALSE))
```

CoordinateCleaner's point references need its own column names (`capital.lon`, `centroid.lon`, `decimalLongitude`); here the longitude and latitude columns are found by name in any of the common spellings. Its `cc_coun()` reads one code column chosen with `ref_col`; here every code column present is matched. With the same reference points and polygons the two packages give the same flags, up to the buffer-polygon band described in the article Coming from CoordinateCleaner; the package tests check this for `institution` and `sea`.
